summary: Psalm 97 announces that Yahweh reigns and calls the whole earth, even distant islands, to rejoice. The poem pictures his rule with clouds, fire, lightning, trembling earth, melting mountains, and public glory, then contrasts idols with Yahweh’s exalted rule. It ends by calling those who love Yahweh to hate evil, trust his preservation, and give thanks.
whyItMatters: In Book IV of Psalms, this chapter belongs to the repeated claim that Yahweh’s reign is more secure than any human throne. It turns cosmic images of judgment into a call for gladness, loyalty, and thanks.

context.author: Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections; this chapter has no named author.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that adopted the Psalms for public and private prayer.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to all Psalms, or to this chapter from this chapter alone, would be misleading.
context.setting: Book IV of Psalms, where poems emphasize Yahweh’s kingship, creation, and enduring rule. The chapter names Zion and the daughters of Judah within a poem that also addresses the whole earth.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry in translation, using parallel lines, vivid images, summons to rejoice, and commands to worship, hate evil, be glad, and give thanks.

outline.heading: The earth is summoned to rejoice
outline.note: Yahweh’s reign is announced, with joy for the earth and islands, while righteousness and justice are named as the foundation of his throne.

outline.heading: Creation trembles before him
outline.note: Fire, lightning, the earth, and mountains show Yahweh’s overwhelming presence as Lord of the whole earth.

outline.heading: The heavens and peoples see his glory
outline.note: The heavens declare his righteousness, the peoples see his glory, and idol worshipers are shamed before him.

outline.heading: Zion rejoices in Yahweh’s judgments
outline.note: Zion and the daughters of Judah respond with gladness because Yahweh is exalted above all the earth and above all gods.

outline.heading: The righteous are called to thankful joy
outline.note: Those who love Yahweh are told to hate evil, are assured of his preserving and delivering care, and are called to glad thanksgiving.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh reigns! Let the earth rejoice! Let the multitude of islands be glad!
keyVerses.why: This opening line states the chapter’s main claim and immediately gives it worldwide scope.

keyVerses.text: Clouds and darkness are around him. Righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne.
keyVerses.why: The verse holds mystery and moral order together: Yahweh is hidden in clouds and darkness, yet his rule rests on righteousness and justice.

keyVerses.text: Let all them be shamed who serve engraved images, who boast in their idols. Worship him, all you gods!
keyVerses.why: This verse marks the chapter’s sharp contrast between Yahweh’s reign and the claims attached to idols or other gods.

keyVerses.text: You who love Yahweh, hate evil! He preserves the souls of his saints. He delivers them out of the hand of the wicked.
keyVerses.why: The poem turns from cosmic praise to the response expected from Yahweh’s people: moral rejection of evil and trust in his preserving care.

themes: Righteousness and justice as the throne’s foundation
Light and gladness for the righteous

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by saying, “Yahweh reigns”?
questions.answer: The chapter presents Yahweh as king over the whole earth, not only over one place or one people. That claim is shown through commands for the earth and islands to rejoice, through creation trembling before him, and through his exaltation above all gods.

questions.question: Why are “clouds and darkness” around him?
questions.answer: The image presents Yahweh’s presence as overwhelming and not fully visible or manageable. The same verse also says righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne, so the darkness does not mean moral confusion; it means the ruler is beyond ordinary human control or inspection.

questions.question: Are the fire, lightning, and melting mountains meant as literal weather reports?
questions.answer: The chapter uses creation imagery to portray Yahweh’s power and presence. Fire goes before him, lightning lights up the world, the earth trembles, and mountains melt like wax; the poem’s point is that even the most stable parts of creation cannot resist the Lord of the whole earth.

questions.question: Who are the “gods” in verse 7?
questions.answer: The verse addresses the world of idols and divine rivals in poetic language: those who serve engraved images are shamed, and “all you gods” are commanded to worship Yahweh. Readers differ on whether the line imagines heavenly beings, the supposed powers represented by idols, or a poetic way of declaring Yahweh’s superiority; the chapter itself emphasizes that Yahweh is exalted far above all gods.

questions.question: What are “engraved images” and “idols” doing in this psalm?
questions.answer: They represent rival objects of worship and boasting. The chapter contrasts them with Yahweh’s visible glory and exalted rule, saying those who serve and boast in them should be shamed.

questions.question: Why does Zion rejoice at Yahweh’s judgments?
questions.answer: In the chapter, Yahweh’s judgments are not presented as random punishment but as the actions of the ruler whose throne is founded on righteousness and justice. Zion and the daughters of Judah are glad because those judgments show Yahweh’s rule over the earth and above all gods.

questions.question: Does “hate evil” mean hating people?
questions.answer: The verse commands those who love Yahweh to hate evil, not to treat personal hatred as a virtue. In the same line, the chapter says Yahweh preserves his saints and delivers them from the hand of the wicked, so the contrast is between loyalty to Yahweh and participation in evil.

questions.question: What does “Light is sown for the righteous” mean?
questions.answer: The image treats light as something planted for the righteous, paired with gladness for the upright in heart. The chapter does not explain the timing or mechanism; it gives a poetic assurance that those aligned with righteousness are not left without light and joy.

questions.question: How does the chapter end?
questions.answer: It ends with a direct call to gladness and thanks: righteous people are told to be glad in Yahweh and give thanks to his holy Name. That ending gathers the chapter’s movement from universal kingship and judgment into worshipful response.

glossary.def: Distant lands or coastlands included in the chapter’s opening summons to rejoice when Yahweh reigns.
The image of royal rule; in this chapter its foundation is righteousness and justice.
Made objects served in worship, contrasted here with Yahweh’s glory and exalted rule.
The named place that hears and is glad because of Yahweh’s judgments.
Those belonging to Yahweh in the verse that says he preserves their souls and delivers them from the wicked.
The name of Yahweh as the focus of thanks in the chapter’s final line.
